blocks.text: In Succa 5b the giant bird (§. 502), as the extreme of size, is set against the צפרתא, similar to the juxtaposition of the two extremes of the unicorn and lice nits (§. 174), and so צפורתא, with the diminutive ending תא, may denote a very small little bird, perhaps the hummingbird. Perhaps it is also meant in the passage (Temura 34a) in which it is said that it was customary to embroider the figure of birds on purses or similar objects made of hair. In any case צפורתא denotes all kinds of small birds, similar to some other names by which small birds are called; cf. the following article.

We mention here some other names by which small kinds of birds are generally called. The frequently occurring פרגיות is explained in various ways: by Raschi on B. mez. 24b as גוזלות, which does not necessarily mean young pigeons, but simply young ones, here young small birds (see §. 1). On Berachoth 39a Raschi translates it as פרדריש, Perdrix, partridge, but inaccurately, although partridges do indeed also belong to the delicacies prepared from the flesh of young birds. The biblical אשתעשע (Ps. 119, 16) is rendered by the Chaldean as אתפרג "to delight oneself". Perhaps one should think of a kind of fricassee, stewed meat, from Frigo.
The Aruch explains the word as: תרנגולים קטנים "young chickens" and, still more generally, as: צפרים קטנים "young birds".
In the Midrasch Rabba (Bereschit fol. 19, col. 4) young fowl are called פרגין, and Rabba (Echa fol. 59, col. 3): פריגין (cf. also Tos. Chulin 62b. s.v. כרזי).
Another general name for young fowl is פרפראות (Berachoth 42a). Cf. Buxdorf (Lex. p. 1846), and צלצלא, cf. §. 252.
נעמית (Kelim 17, 14), נעמיתא (Sabbat 110b), בת נעמיתא (M. Katan 26a), בת יענה and בת יענה (Chulin 64b), pl. נעמיות (Rabba [p. 189] Bamidbar fol. 247, c).

In the first passage a vessel is mentioned that is made from a glazed ostrich egg. Such an egg has the contents of 24 hens' eggs and is therefore of considerable size (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 342). The contents of the egg were used in medicine (Sabbat 110b). The belief that the ostrich lives on indigestible things such as glass, iron and the like was erroneous; thus the Talmud calls broken glass the food of the ostrich (ibid. 128a); what is correct in it, however, is that the ostrich, owing to its poor sense of taste, swallows such objects, yet it lives on vegetable matter, which it consumes without discrimination; for which reason the statement of the Midrasch (Jalk. Schim. part 2, fol. 17a) that the ostriches devoured the flesh of the slain Agag is incorrect.

In the passage Chulin 64b it is said of the ostrich that it stays with its young and mourns their loss. However, it is known that the ostrich in the tropical zone merely presses a hollow into the sand and leaves the hatching of the eggs to the sun. It lays near the nest a separate egg, which it tramples, so that the contents putrefy and produce maggots, on which the hatched ostriches live at first; nevertheless it is correct that on either side of the tropics it broods itself and defends nest and young with much courage.

The well-known stupidity of our bird may perhaps underlie the statement of Nachmanides (on Job 30, 29) that the ostrich remains silent even when it is beaten. Regarding the voracity of the bird mentioned above, let it be added that it once snatched away a Rabbi's prayer straps, whereupon he strangled it (Jerusalem Talmud M. Katan fol. 83b), and that pieces of gold bars the size of olives were thrown to it, which it swallowed and then passed out polished (Rabba Bamidbar fol. 247, c), in which connection one should think of the grinding down of the metal by the muscular stomach of the bird. In the Jerusalem Talmud (Joma ch. 4, Hal. 4) it is stated in more detail: the pieces of gold were coated with dough and thrown to the ostriches, which swallowed them and thereby cleansed them (מסננין).

טוס (B. Kama 55a) טוס (Sabbat 130a), and in the parallel passage (Chulin 116a): טוסא. Gr. Ταώς [Taōs], just as Raschi [p. 190] on the first and last passages translates the word as פוואן, Paon; the female: טוסמ (Jerusalem Talmud B. Kama 5a). In the first passage it is said that one may not crossbreed the domestic hen and the peacock, although they are raised together.

In the two other passages it is related that someone served his guest the head of a peacock cooked in milk (or perhaps with milk set out at the same time), which he also ate, because in that place it was permitted to eat fowl cooked with milk.

That the head and not another part of the body was prepared as a tasty dish may have its reason in that the head is perhaps the tastiest part of the peacock, for its flesh is anything but that; it is rather hard and lean, and the bird is kept only for ornament (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 306). From our passage it follows at the same time that the peacock is a clean bird; nevertheless it is not now declared clean; cf. Landau (Aruch s.v. נגר). Cf. p. 184,
אוז (B. mez. 91b), אווזא (Joma 84a*), pl. אוזין (Sebachim 70b), קוקא (from quacking, §. 108, pl. קאקי, Gittin 73a).
